Perhaps this explains why Sohrawardî did not accept Avicennian angelology’s claim that each Angel is a unique individual constituting a species in itself. Thomas Aquinas likewise held this view, and Leibniz drew inspiration from it. For Sohrawardî, an angelic being is defined not by constituting a species individually in the Peripatetic sense, but by the degree of intensity of its radiance. Intensity is thus introduced into the very category of substance. A soul may be “more a soul,” or “more intensely a soul,” than another (Motârahât, § 66, referring to Plato). The degree of intensity ultimately establishes an individuation just as precise as the definition by species taught by Avicennism and Thomism. It also leaves open the way of ascent from one degree of intensity to the next. We cannot pursue this comparison of angelologies further here. See also Prolegomena II, pp. 46 ff. ↩

The mysterious book given to Chrétien by Count Philip of Flanders has sometimes been too readily dismissed as a literary fiction, and the importance of the silentium mysticum—the mystical silence observed by the hermit when teaching the secret prayer—has been underestimated. Even if we found only affinities, rather than “sources” in the historical sense, the Grail cycle would require a different interpretation from one that, through piety or habit, merely discovers the teachings of the official Church there, whether symbolically or otherwise.
